# Pilot — NYC Capital Projects (Socrata)

**Real data.** Generated by `tools/adapters/projects-nyc-capital.py` from
[NYC Open Data, Capital Projects](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Capital-Projects/n7gv-k5yt)
(Socrata `n7gv-k5yt`, Mayor's Office of Operations): major infrastructure and IT projects of
$25M or more.

```bash
python3 tools/adapters/projects-nyc-capital.py --limit 400 --out examples/pilot-nyc-capital
```

Result: **363 projects** and 44 agencies, all passing JSON Schema, reference integrity and
the SHACL shapes. The dataset's metadata carries no licence field. Check NYC Open Data's
terms of use before redistributing the converted files.

## The dataset is a time series, not a list of projects

The first reading of the metadata was 3,320 rows, so 3,320 projects. Wrong. The dataset holds
**24 reporting snapshots from 2013-09 to 2023-01**, and each project appears once per
snapshot: project 101 appears 24 times. Converting every row produced one project per row and
hundreds of duplicate `@id`s, which the validator rejected. The adapter now converts only
the latest snapshot (2023-01-01, 363 projects).

The history is real and the profile cannot carry it. Project 101's forecast completion
across snapshots:

| Reported | Phase | Forecast completion |
|---|---|---|
| 2013-09 | Design | 2018-02 |
| 2015-02 | Construction Procurement | 2023-01 |
| 2015-08 | Construction | 2019-05 |
| 2019-01 | Construction | 2020-08 |
| 2022-09 | Construction | 2023-08 |

The profile holds the current value of each field. A publisher with snapshots like these has
no place to put the earlier ones. That is a limitation to record rather than a field to add
now: history could be an `Article` per snapshot, or a versioned record. Left for a pilot
with a publisher that needs it.

## The data is old

The newest snapshot is dated **2023-01-01**. The dataset's own metadata shows it last
updated in 2025, but no snapshot has been added since 2023. So `status: active` is true as of
that date, and many of these projects have probably finished since. Each converted project
carries `dateModified: 2023-01-01`, so a consumer can see how old the record is.

## Status is inferred from the dataset's scope

The source publishes no status column. The dataset is defined as *projects currently active
in design, procurement or construction*, so every converted project is `status: active`.
That comes from the dataset's description, not from a value in any row.

## Phases are the publisher's own, and the field is untidy

Phases in the latest snapshot:

| Source `current_phase` | Projects | Converted |
|---|---|---|
| Design | 141 | yes |
| Construction | 154 | yes |
| Construction Procurement | 47 | yes |
| IT | 9 | **omitted**: not a lifecycle stage |
| blank | 12 | omitted |

Two findings:

- **Capital projects use their own lifecycle**, and the profile handled it without change. The
  adapter declares a `DefinedTermSet` (`capital-project-phase`) and projects reference its
  terms. This is the capital-project test the profile was designed against: nothing in it
  assumed software.
- **`IT` is a kind of project, not a stage.** The source mixes category into the phase
  column. The adapter drops it and counts it rather than invent a phase.

The set also includes `Close-Out`, which appears in earlier snapshots only. It is
declared from the source's values, not from this snapshot's.

## Other source gaps

| Gap | Projects |
|---|---|
| `forecast_completion` blank, so no `expectedEndDate` | 28 |
| `design_start` blank, so no `startDate` | 22 |

`startDate` is `design_start`, when design began, which may be earlier than any date a person
would call the project's start (project 101: 2003). It is the earliest date the source gives.
Phase, dates and organizations are all optional in the profile, so none of these blank rows
failed validation, which is the profile's intent: real publishers have gaps.

## Not carried

`category`, `borough`, budget forecast and budget and schedule changes. Category and borough
are plausible additions if more pilots want them. Budget figures belong in the `budget`
profile.

## Agencies are mostly codes, and there is no register

The source publishes one string per agency, and it mixes forms: codes (`DOT`, `DEP`, `DDC`),
names (`Parks & Recreation`, `Sanitation`) and the same body twice (`Police` and `NYPD`,
`HHC`, `H+H` and `Health & Hospitals Corporation (HHC)`). Some entries are not agencies
(`n/a`) or are joint (`NYPD & FDNY`, `DCAS/CTS`). Unlike GOV.UK, no register of New York City
agencies turned up in a search of NYC Open Data, so there is nothing authoritative to resolve against.

What the adapter does:

- The code is kept in its own field: an `identifier` (`local:nyc-agency-code`).
- For 14 common codes the adapter supplies the official name (`DOT` is the Department of
  Transportation). **Those names come from the adapter, not the source.** The table is in
  the script and should be checked before relying on it. The code also goes in `alternateName`.
- The other 30 agencies keep the code, or the string as written, as their `name`.
- `n/a` is dropped as not an agency.
- Joint entries and duplicate spellings (`Police` and `NYPD`) are not merged.

A client agency is mapped to `member` (participating), the managing agency to
`parentOrganization` (responsible).
